candidate.answerReason: Consecutive pairs form a geometric series with first term 1+√2/4 and common ratio 1/4. Its limiting sum is (4+√2)/3.

methods.label: Group consecutive terms into geometric pairs
methods.explanation:
Although the individual terms do not have a constant ratio, consecutive pairs do. Group the terms as
\[
\left(1+\frac{\sqrt2}{4}\right)
+\left(\frac14+\frac{\sqrt2}{16}\right)
+\left(\frac1{16}+\frac{\sqrt2}{64}\right)+\cdots.
\]
Each pair is one fourth of the preceding pair. Let \(a=1+\sqrt2/4\), and let \(S_n\) be the total of the first \(n\) complete pairs. Multiplying this finite geometric sum by \(1/4\) and subtracting cancels the interior terms:
\[
S_n-\frac14S_n=a-a4^{-n}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
S_n=\frac{4+\sqrt2}{3}\left(1-4^{-n}\right).
\]
Because \(0<1/4<1\), the quantity \(4^{-n}\) tends to zero. Every term is positive, so a partial total ending between complete pairs lies between the neighboring complete-pair totals and has the same limit. The limiting length is therefore
\[
\frac{4+\sqrt2}{3}\text{ inches},
\]
choice D.
methods.levelReason: A finite geometric-sum calculation and the decay of powers of 1/4 justify the infinite sum using precalculus reasoning.
